overview.title: The Wildsea - The setting and the game
overview.subtitle_bottom: On the setting and the focus of the game
overview.card1_item1: The Verdancy: Around three hundred years ago, the world's empires were toppled by a furious wave of green, a tide of untrammelled growth that spilled over from the west. That event gave rise to the Wildsea: a titanic expanse of whispering waves and inextricable branches.
overview.card1_item2: Ships and their crews: Vessels propelled by chainsaws and other machinery carve their way through the dense waves of vegetation. Their crews are motley: the hardened descendants of humanity mingle with cactoid gunslingers, animated wrecks, colonies of silk-clad spiders, human-looking slugs with wooden bones adrift and other even stranger things.
overview.card1_item3: Ports and settlements: Outcrops of ancient land and old-world monuments now serve as ports, cities, farms and prisons, each with its own laws and customs. Ancient cultures have fragmented into new and often unrecognisable forms.
overview.card1_item4: Economy: The economies of this world are unpredictable and shifting, but there is always valuable stuff to be found for those willing to brave the dangers of the wild.
overview.card2_item1: Your character: You are an wildsailor, a member of a crew that carves its way through the wilds aboard a ship of its own.
overview.card2_item2: Focus of play: Exploration, progress and change. You will define the world of the Wildsea as you sail it. You will face survivor cultures and wild beasts, and seek out wrecks, cargo, rumours and secrets.
overview.card2_item3: Hooks and arcs: Adventures begin as hooks, elements from the setting or a character's history with the potential to bloom into an arc: a story for you and your crew to experience. Arcs, along with the triumphs and disasters within them, will let you develop your character.
overview.card2_item4: The conversation: Decisions are made through a collaborative process that brings the players together to resolve an event.
overview.card2_item5: The Firefly: The game director in the Wildsea is there to ask the right questions and keep the flow of the conversation, as well as to arbitrate the rules as needed.

core.title: The Wildsea - Core concepts
core.subtitle_bottom: Guide to the world and its inhabitants
core.card1_intro: This page highlights the most important aspects of the world.
core.card1_item1: The treetops are a sea: Though made of branches and leaves rather than water, the treetops are like a traditional sea in many ways; there are waves (formed by the natural contours of the arboreal canopy), ports (built on the little solid ground remaining) and a vast number of ships (their hulls held aloft by the branches). Though it is possible to move through the canopy without a ship, doing so for any length of time is a huge risk.
core.card1_item2: Land is scarce and valuable: Mountain tops and great chunks of earth or debris trapped in the canopy act as islands and archipelagos, fiercely protected by their inhabitants. Settlements built on these outcrops are designed more for safety than comfort, giving them a ramshackle appearance and multiple layers of defence against the menacing waves.
core.card1_item3: Plant growth is uncontrolled: The sea's plants grow at a frenetic rate when connected to the Ironroot, the network of colossal trees that form the base of the canopy you will sail. A cut branch will lie inert, but another will grow in its place within hours. The topography changes constantly and, from time to time, an unexpected surge of growth claims a ship or a colony.
core.card1_item4: Open flames are forbidden: Nearly every culture forbids the use of fire while out at the sea, for good reason. Flames burn slowly in the wood of the Wildsea and spread at a terrifying speed. If a fire breaks out, even the most bitter enemies will set aside their differences to fight it together.
core.card1_item5: Crezzerin corrupts on contact: Secreted by the most dangerous vegetation of the Wildsea, Crezzerin is a potent toxin. The merest contact does little more than burn the skin, but long-term exposure warps both body and mind in terrifying ways.
core.card2_intro: Whimsical. Beautiful. Dangerous. There are many ways to describe the waves of branches and leaves of the Wildsea, but no single word does them justice. They are a tangle of life, or many lives; nature at war with civilisation and with itself, a whirlwind of growth in motion.
core.card2_item1: The motion: The first thing most people notice is the motion. Whether from the sighing of high-altitude winds or the bustle of beasts and insects, the canopy of the Wildsea never rests. The effect is similar to that of the old salt sea, with swells and tides. Even an anchored ship keeps rocking as the branches rise and fall beneath its hull.
core.card2_item2: The sound: The second thing you will notice is the sound. The Wildsea is never silent. There is the constant rustle of leaves, the creaking of branches, the buzz of countless insects, the calls of birds and lemurs, and the shouts of sailors at the rail. Arboreal sea shanties are sung and the hearts of ships rumble deep within their hulls. Life makes noise, and the Wildsea is full of life.
core.card2_item3: The danger: Not everything that dwells in the waves wants to kill you, but enough of it does. There are beasts that hunt ships, eager to feed on the aftermath of their wrecks. Insects build hives in wood and flesh in inscrutable ways. Even spirits hunt and are hunted in turn. And, as a presence beneath the layers of prey and predation, leviathans lurk, waiting for their moment.
core.card3_intro: Some make the mistake of thinking the waves are little more than a tapestry of trees, but nothing could be further from the truth: the world of the Wildsea is a world of life and growth, with all the diversity that entails.
core.card3_item1: Vegetal diversity: The ships of the east cut through giant cactus pads, their hulls reinforced against the relentless spines. Other places are covered in devouring fungi, bogged down by burps of noxious gas or smothered by stalks of grass a kilometre tall. In Terminus, branches strike down like railway tracks; in Belltower, brass grows and flowers sing.
core.card3_item2: The depths: The deeper you travel, the more present the immensity of the sea becomes. There is a pressure that mounts as you descend; not physical, but rather mental. As you dive beneath the canopy, you travel not only through space but through history, passing from light into a darkness of ruins and mysteries, of unearthed relics. The branches snake around the secrets of bygone eras. Knowledge itself carries weight, and those driven to dive train themselves not to bend beneath it.
core.card3_item3: What came before?: Nobody really knows. The oldest inhabitants of the Wildsea have only scattered memories, for their bodies outlast their minds. Some, woken from amber, recall the old world as if it were a dream. Others rely on scraps of tapestry or mildewed books. Whatever knowledge people have of the past is what the sea chooses to give, or what they can dredge from the deepest places. Most have grown used to living in the present, using whatever they can without trying to understand the mysteries behind their finds.

glossary.title: The Wildsea - Glossary
glossary.subtitle_bottom: Terms and vocabulary of the world
glossary.card1_item1: Verdancy: The apocalyptic event that ended the previous era 300 years ago.
glossary.card1_item2: Crezzerin: A toxic substance directly linked to the Verdancy, though how is unknown.
glossary.card1_item3: The Conflagration: A region in the north where a terrible fire burns, seeming to threaten to consume the whole world (hence the taboo against open-sky flames).
glossary.card2_item1: A crew member fallen overboard is never considered dead until their body is recovered or a full winter has passed. There are too many stories of wildsailors turning up in the ports of Thrashside, mud-caked and Crezzerin-covered, who crawled mile after mile of waves in search of their old crews.
glossary.card2_item2: Looking north while out on the open Wildsea is bad luck, as it often offers a view of the distant blackened blot of the Conflagration, the greatest shame of the post-green world.
glossary.card2_item3: The first sip of a drink or the first bite must be spat into the waves. It is unclear whether this tradition began as an offering to the Wildsea or as a safety precaution against Crezzerin contamination.
glossary.card2_item4: The bodies of wildsailors who died, whether by accident or old age, may be dealt with in many ways, depending on their cultures and beliefs in life, but for those without families or final wishes, letting them drop through a rift is one of the most respectful ways to pay tribute to the fallen.
glossary.card2_item5: Wearing green clothes or carrying a sporescarf dyed that colour invites ruin: if you fall overboard you will be harder to spot.
glossary.card3_item1: Wildsea: The sea of vegetation covering the surface of the planet.
glossary.card3_item2:
Layers of the Wildsea:
  • The Skies
    A wide blue firmament stretches over the Wildsea: the Skies host insects, birds and the occasional airship, though strong winds and storms make reliable aerial travel impossible. Most of those who settle in the Skies take up residence on plateaus, mountainsides or floating cities.
  • The Thrash
    The highest layer of the iron-rooted trees that form the Wildsea. The Thrash is a place of life and trade, a forest canopy dotted with mountain peaks, shipwreck reefs and improvised cities. What remains of civilisation is concentrated mostly in these last fragments of land, and ships sail the seas of leaves around them.
  • The Tangle
    Although the Thrash is dense enough to be sailed, it is in the Tangle where most ships rest their hulls, where the branches begin to weave together in great depth. Life, insects, animals and other beings thrive in the warmth of that twilight, and it can be travelled with relative safety given enough preparation and skill.
  • The Sink
    Where ships run aground and leviathans hold sway. As dense as the Tangle but far more dangerous, the Sink takes its name from the treacherous branches that compose it: whether by natural or artificial means, most vessels that descend into the Sink find it almost impossible to return to the surface.
  • The Drown
    The point of no return, where there are no branches left to hold you, only enormous trunks, where light dies. The trunks of the Ironroot stand in the darkness, set apart from one another by impossible distances. There are great swathes of the Drown that have never been touched by sunlight, which reaches only through a few cracks.
  • The Darkness-Under-Eaves
    The roots of the sea and the bones of the old world. The less known about this place, the better.
glossary.card3_item3: Canopy: Another colloquial name for the Wildsea.
glossary.card3_item4: Waves: The ocean swells formed by the foliage.
glossary.card3_item6: Tallshank: A tree that rises above all the others like a tower almost touching the clouds.
glossary.card3_item7: Spits: More or less ephemeral colonies that sail adrift over the canopy.
glossary.card3_item8: Islands: Solid ground unlikely to be swallowed by the waves.
glossary.card3_item9: Reefs: Outcrops of wreckage that may hold riches to discover but are very dangerous.
glossary.card3_item10: Rifts Openings through which one can fall to the deeper layers, perhaps even all the way to the Ironroot.
glossary.card4_item2: Navigator: They know how to read the patterns of the Wildsea, whether a wave current will hold the ship or sink it.
glossary.card4_item3: Sporescarf: A garment that protects against any harmful particles in the lower layers (spores, Crezzerin, etc.).
glossary.card4_item4: Wavewalkers: Folk who have managed to dive the Wildsea without a ship.
glossary.card4_item5: Mire: An wildsailor's personal baggage, which can sometimes drag them to the darkest bottom.
glossary.card4_item6: Wake: The gap a ship leaves when crossing the Wildsea.
glossary.card4_item7: Lookout: The watchperson's post at the top of the ship, usually on the mainmast.
glossary.card4_item8: Bow, stern, port, starboard: The front, back, left and right of the ship (facing forward) respectively.
glossary.card5_item1: Ardents: Direct descendants of the humans who survived by retreating to high places.
glossary.card5_item2: Ektus: Creatures that blend humanoid and cactoid.
glossary.card5_item3: Gau: Fungal beings that are not born but cultivated.
glossary.card5_item4: Tzelicrae: Colonies of spiders that behave as a single being (though they speak of themselves in the plural).
glossary.card5_item6: Ketra: Descendants of humans, but trapped in the Darkness-Under-Eaves for generations, mutated by Crezzerin in monstrous ways, in body and soul.
glossary.card5_item7: Mothryn: Winged creatures whose wings are not entirely useless but do not let them fly either, perhaps a little gliding.

bloodlines.title: The Wildsea - Bloodlines
bloodlines.subtitle_bottom: Guide to the world and its inhabitants
bloodlines.card1_intro: The four most common bloodlines across the waves are the Ardents, the Ektus, the Gau and the Tzelicrae. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses and adapts in its own way to life in the treetops.
bloodlines.card1_item1: The Ardents: The descendants of ancient humanity, forged by hardship and disaster. The culture, traditions and appearance of the Ardents are as varied as those of their ancestors, but they share a common trait: perseverance. They are a race of survivors; tough, weathered and attuned to the spiritual elements of the waves.
bloodlines.card1_item2: The Ektus: Fibrous cactoids from the east of Ictherine. The forest-world tore the Ektus away from the dunes and waterfalls of their ancestral home. Today most sail the seas, determined to reclaim their place in a world that tried to erase them. Though Ektus bodies take many forms, they tend to exceed the other bloodlines in height and bulk.
bloodlines.card1_item3: The Gau: The Gau are not born, but cultivated in the warm darkness of fungal colonies before being sent into the world when they reach maturity. Though each surviving colony has its own traditions and biological quirks, curiosity and an adventurous spirit are common traits among the Gau.
bloodlines.card1_item4: The Tzelicrae: Each Tzelicrae is a hive-mind of thousands of spiders that has shaped, negotiated or stolen a humanoid body. Many Tzelicrae weave a silken exterior or inhabit cast-off clothing and armour, like a hermit crab in its shell. A fortunate few win the skin lottery, which lets them pass unnoticed among the communities of other bloodlines.
bloodlines.card2_intro: Though they are the most common, the four central bloodlines are far from the only species adapted to life in the rustling waves. In recent years, three others have become more notable.
bloodlines.card2_item1: The Ironbound: The souls of wrecked ships sometimes gather the material of the shattered hulls around them and create a body with which to escape the solitude of the waves. These flickering minds call themselves Ironbound. Some mistake them for machines, but in truth they are as capable of learning and feeling as any other living being.
bloodlines.card2_item2: The Ketra: Like the Ardents, the Ketra descend from a humanity subjected to the vicissitudes of history. In their case, they were trapped beneath the jungles when the Verdancy swept the world, in the heart of the mountains and in industrial buildings large enough to resist the growing roots. Exposure to Crezzerin and dampness transformed them into something very different from their Ardent kin.
bloodlines.card2_item3: The Mothryn: Short-lived but determined to fill their time with meaning, the Mothryn are fast, fragile and often lavishly decorated. They wear bright colours and elaborate clothing, a direct result of their history of monastic isolation. Though they have wings, they lack the ability to fly; most can only glide, but they can rise on updrafts.

rolls.title: The Wildsea - Roll summary
rolls.card1_intro: Six-sided dice are rolled and the pool can hold a maximum of six dice.
rolls.card1_item1: You can only use one skill or language per roll.
rolls.card1_item2: Advantages can come from gear, surroundings, resources or a companion's help.
rolls.card2_rule1: Cut x: Ignore x number of dice starting with the highest values.
rolls.card2_rule2: Trade cut for impact: Each die of cut taken adds one impact.
rolls.card3_item1: Two wildsailors join for one roll: one brings edge/advantages and the other skills.
rolls.card3_item2: Shared risk: Both suffer the negative consequences of a conflict or disaster.
rolls.card4_banner:
If you have no dice in your pool, roll 2d
and keep the lowest.
rolls.card5_title: Interpreting the results of a roll
rolls.card5_act_6: 6 = triumph: You achieve your goal and gain an advantage.
rolls.card5_react_6: 6 = triumph: You avoid all damage, effects or loss of position.
rolls.card5_act_54: 5-4 = conflict: You achieve your goal, but there are consequences or complications.
rolls.card5_react_54: 5-4 = conflict: You avoid the worst, but suffer some minor damage or complication.
rolls.card5_act_321: 3-2-1 = disaster: You fail to achieve your goal and suffer serious consequences.
rolls.card5_react_321: 3-2-1 = disaster: You take all the damage and suffer serious consequences.
rolls.card5_act_doubles: Doubles = twist: A relevant unexpected change occurs (in combat, impact +1).
rolls.card5_react_doubles: Doubles = twist: You deal damage to the attacker.
